title: The Houles cross from Quebec to Minnesota
summary: Quebec, then Michigan, then Centerville, read off the birthplaces of one household.
paragraphs: The 1875 Minnesota state census caught the whole thing on one page. Michel Houle, seventy, born Lower Canada. His son John B., thirty-two, born Lower Canada. John B.'s wife Virginia Tourville, twenty-eight, born Lower Canada. Then the children: Philias, seven, born Michigan. John A., six, Theodore, four, Thomas, three, and William, one, all born Minnesota.
Read in order, that is the route. Quebec until at least the 1840s, Michigan around 1868, Minnesota from about 1869 onward. The Michigan leg is new; no earlier account of this family had it.
Michel's age puts his birth at about 1805, within a year of the 1806 the earlier research claimed for him, which is the first independent support that story has had.

Michel's own dates are now known: born 29 September 1802, died 6 December 1898 at Centerville. So he crossed in his forties or early fifties with children in tow, and lived another four decades on this side.
What is still missing is the crossing itself. No passenger list, no border record, and no Quebec parish register has been matched to any of them.

title: The Morkerts move from Ohio into Indiana
summary: A move visible only in the birthplace column of one census page.
paragraphs: Elias Morkert was born in Ohio about 1821 and Elizabeth in Ohio in 1828. By 1880 they are farming in Clay Township, Carroll County, Indiana, with sons born in Indiana. Henry Morkert, born in Indiana about 1851, gives both his parents as Ohio-born on the same census.

There is one Ohio record now. The 1820 census has a Jno L. Morkert at Gratis in Preble County, on the Indiana line, the year before Elias was born in Ohio, and Morkerts appear again in the Preble County deed books through 1831.

Elizabeth's parents are recorded as born in Pennsylvania, which sets the family's direction: Pennsylvania, then Ohio, then Indiana, the standard route for German-speaking farming families in those decades.
The surnames agree. Morkert is German or Alsatian; Burkhalter is Swiss German.

title: John A. Houle is born at Centerville
summary: The first person on the Houle line born in America.
paragraphs: His death record in 1942 gives the birthplace plainly: Centerville, Minnesota, in 1868, to John B. Houle and Virginia Tourville. That one line does two jobs. It names the generation above him, and it proves the family was settled in the village by then rather than still moving.
He died at Forest Lake Township seventy-four years later, about fifteen miles from where he was born.

title: The Morkerts turn up in Alabama
summary: One census page, and a leg of the family's history nobody had.
paragraphs: Henry N. Morkert, 59, Mary M., 53, and Archibald, 22, are enumerated at Foley and Magnolia Springs on the Alabama Gulf coast in 1910. The birthplaces on the same page hold the whole story of the family to that point: Henry born Indiana, Mary born Ohio, Archibald born Indiana.
Every earlier account of this family goes straight from Indiana to North Dakota. This page says they went south first.
Nothing explains why, and nothing yet says how long. Within seven years they were in North Dakota.

title: The Morkerts settle at Leeds, North Dakota
summary: Forty years in one county, and the longest stretch this family stayed anywhere.
paragraphs: Archibald registered for the WWI draft in Benson County, was farming at Leeds with Julia and four children in 1930, registered again in 1942, and was still there in the 1950 census. His father Henry died at Leeds in 1933 and is buried there.
Julia was born in North Dakota, which means she was already local when they married. Their children, Helen, William, Clarence and Orris, were all born in the state.

This is where the surname fractures. The 1930 census writes the family as Morhert at Leeds and Marbert at York, the same county in the same year, which is why none of this was findable by searching for Morkert.

title: John J. Houle marries Lydia Bernier
summary: The marriage that produced Lloyd, and the one that corrects the whole Houle line.
paragraphs: She was seventeen or eighteen, he was twenty-two. Their son Lloyd was born three years later.

This record matters out of proportion to the wedding, because earlier research had Lloyd's father as a different man entirely, a David Houle born at Fort Ripley in 1884. The 1930 census puts Lloyd in John J. and Lydia's household at Forest Lake, and John J.'s own death record names his parents. David is not in this family.
Everything that used to hang off David, including a line back to Quebec, came off the tree with him. Michel Houle then came back by a different route.

title: Lloyd Houle marries Blanche LaCasse
summary: Two French-Canadian families from the same county, joined three weeks before Pearl Harbor.
paragraphs: He was twenty-four and from Forest Lake; she was twenty-five and from Centerville. Their daughter Susan was born in February 1949 and appears as a one year old in the census the following spring.
They were married sixty-four years. Blanche died in 2007 and Lloyd in 2015 at ninety-eight, and they are buried together at Calvary Cemetery in Forest Lake.

title: Orris brings the family to Minnesota
summary: The move that put a North Dakota farming family in the same town as a Quebec one.
paragraphs: Orris was born at Leeds in 1923 and died in Minnesota in 2011, and the Forest Lake area is where his obituary and his children place him. Exactly when he left North Dakota has not been documented here; earlier research says after the war, which fits a man who registered for the draft at nineteen in 1942.
Without this move there is no marriage between Rodney and Susan, and no family on either side of this site.

Evelyn was a Benson County girl too, born at Harlow in 1922, twenty miles from Leeds. She is buried at Scandinavian Cemetery in Forest Lake, which is where the Norwegian side of this family shows up in the landscape.

title: Rodney Morkert marries Susan Houle
summary: The day the two halves of this site became one family.
paragraphs: Everything above this on the Morkert side starts in Ohio and comes through Indiana, Alabama and North Dakota. Everything above it on the Houle side starts in Quebec and comes through Centerville. They meet here.

Three children followed: DeAnn in 1969, Kenneth, and Joseph in 1975. All three birth records name Rodney Leo Morkert and Susan Marie Houle as the parents, which is how the two lines are tied together on paper.
The marriage record itself has not been found yet, which is why this is marked as probable rather than proven. The date is inferred from DeAnn's birth in 1969.

title: Joe Morkert dies at twenty-seven
summary: The youngest death on this site, and the record that first mapped the family.
paragraphs: DeAnn's younger brother, born 18 September 1975, died on 20 April 2003. He was living in Fridley and had grown up in Scandia. The funeral was at St. Peter's Catholic Church in Forest Lake.

His obituary is what listed three living generations in one place: parents Rodney and Susan, grandparents Orris, Evelyn, Lloyd and Blanche, his sister DeAnn and brother Kenneth, and four nieces and nephews. Almost everything anyone knew about this side of the family before now traced back to it.

title: Michel Houle dies at ninety-six
summary: The immigrant outlived everyone who could have told us where in Quebec he came from.
paragraphs: Born 29 September 1802 in Lower Canada, died 6 December 1898 at Centerville, buried at Saint Genevieve. He had been in Minnesota more than forty years by then and was still being enumerated there in 1895 at about eighty-nine.

He died two years before Minnesota started registering deaths statewide, which is why there is a memorial and a census entry for him but no death certificate. Anything more about him is in the Saint Genevieve parish register or in Quebec.
Earlier research guessed 1806 to 1898 for him. The death is exactly right and the birth is four years out, which is a fair result for a guess nobody had checked.
